hints: Use the observations to identify the products, the white precipitate is silicon dioxide and the strongly acidic solution shows a strong acid is also formed.
walkthrough:
Link observations to products**
You see a white precipitate forming and the pH is 1 to 2. The white solid is $\text{SiO}_{2}$ and the very acidic solution tells you $\text{HCl}$ is produced. $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ is a liquid that reacts vigorously with cold water.

Balance and add states**
Balance Si, then Cl, then H and O: one $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ needs two $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to make one $\text{SiO}_{2}$ and four $\text{HCl}$. Add states: $\text{SiCl}_{4}(l) + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{SiO}_{2}(s) + 4\text{HCl}(aq)$.

hints: Think of the general name given when a covalent chloride is broken down by water to give an oxide and HCl.
walkthrough:
Recognise reaction with water**
When water breaks up a compound to form new products, with $\text{H}$ going to one part and $\text{OH}$ effectively going to the other, we call this splitting by water. For $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ giving $\text{SiO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$, the name is hydrolysis.

hints: Compare what happens on dissolving, NaCl simply dissolves to a neutral solution while SiCl4 reacts chemically to give acidic products.
Recall how bonding changes across Period 3 chlorides, from giant ionic at Na to simple molecular covalent at Si.
walkthrough:
See why behaviour points to bonding**
$\text{NaCl}$ just disappears to give a neutral pH 7 solution. That fits simple dissolving with no chemical reaction. $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ gives heat, gas bubbles and acid, which fits a covalent molecule being attacked and broken by water.

Assign the bonding types**
$\text{NaCl}$ is a giant ionic lattice, so water can separate the ions without breaking covalent bonds. $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ is a simple covalent molecule, so water can hydrolyse the $\text{Si-Cl}$ covalent bonds.

Final answer: $\text{NaCl}$ has ionic bonding.
$\text{SiCl}_{4}$ has covalent bonding.

hints: Recall how electronegativity increases across Period 3, so compare the position of Na and Si relative to Cl.
Think about what a very large electronegativity difference does to the bonding electrons compared to a smaller difference.
Link large difference to complete transfer of electrons and smaller difference to sharing of electrons.
walkthrough:
Compare electronegativities**
Picture Period 3: Na is on the far left with very low electronegativity, Si is further right with higher electronegativity. Cl is on the far right with high electronegativity. So the gap $\text{Na-Cl}$ is much larger than the gap $\text{Si-Cl}$. In other words, Na is less electronegative than Si.

Explain ionic formation in NaCl**
With that very large difference, Cl pulls the valence electron of Na completely away. Na loses an electron to become $\text{Na}^{+}$ and Cl gains it to become $\text{Cl}^{-}$. That complete transfer is ionic bonding.

Explain covalent formation in SiCl4**
With the smaller difference for $\text{Si-Cl}$, neither atom can completely remove electrons from the other. Instead Si and Cl share pairs of electrons, giving covalent bonds in the tetrahedral $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ molecule.

Final answer: Na is less electronegative than Si, so the electronegativity difference between Na and Cl is larger than between Si and Cl.
In $\text{NaCl}$ there is transfer of electron(s) from Na to Cl to form ions.
In $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ there is sharing of (pairs of) electrons between Si and Cl.

hints: Start with the simple rules, an uncombined element is 0 and H is usually +1 and O is usually -2 in these compounds.
Apply the rule that the sum of oxidation numbers equals zero for a neutral molecule to find Cl in HCl and HClO.
walkthrough:
Assign Cl2 and HCl**
In any uncombined element the oxidation number is 0, so Cl in $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is 0. In $\text{HCl}$, H is +1 and the molecule is neutral, so $+1 + \text{Cl} = 0$, giving Cl = -1.

Assign HClO**
In $\text{HClO}$, H is +1 and O is -2. Let Cl be $x$. Then $$+1 + x -2 = 0$$ so $x = +1$. Chlorine has been both oxidised from 0 to +1 and reduced from 0 to -1.

hints: Notice that the same element, Cl2 at 0, goes to both a higher and a lower oxidation number in the products.
walkthrough:
Spot simultaneous oxidation and reduction**
The same species $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is both oxidised to $+1$ in $\text{HClO}$ and reduced to $-1$ in $\text{HCl}$. When the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, the special name is disproportionation.

hints: Think about what must be removed from drinking water to make it safe, living pathogens that cause disease.
walkthrough:
Link HClO to safe water**
The $\text{HClO}$ formed is a strong oxidising agent that destroys bacteria and other micro-organisms. That is why a small amount of chlorine is added to drinking water, to sterilise it and prevent disease.

hints: Treat the mixture as two separate acids, HCl and HClO, each being neutralised by NaOH to give a sodium salt plus water.
Combine the two neutralisation equations and check that Na, Cl, H and O all balance, the bleach product is NaClO.
walkthrough:
Write the two neutralisations**
Cold dilute $\text{NaOH}$ neutralises acids. First: $$\text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Second: $$\text{NaOH} + \text{HClO} \rightarrow \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ $\text{NaClO}$ is sodium chlorate(I), the bleach.

Combine into one equation**
Add the two equations together: $$2\text{NaOH} + \text{HCl} + \text{HClO} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Check atoms: 2 Na, 2 Cl, 2 O from hydroxides plus 1 O from HClO, and 4 H on each side. It balances.
